headings.title: Introduction to Referencing and Citation in Nursing Research
headings.content: Referencing is the standard practice of acknowledging the authors and sources you use when writing academic papers, research projects, or clinical guidelines. In nursing, where evidence-based practice directly impacts patient safety, citing sources shows the foundation of your claims. Every time you state a fact, borrow an idea, or use statistical data from another writer, you must point directly to them. This system allows other healthcare professionals to trace your information back to the original research, verify its accuracy, and build upon your findings in future clinical studies.

headings.title: Purpose and Importance of Academic Integrity
headings.content: Academic integrity forms the backbone of professional nursing education and practice. Nurses are trusted professionals who must display honesty and accountability in every duty, including writing and research. Plagiarism—presenting someone else's work, words, or ideas as your own—violates this trust. Intentional or accidental plagiarism undermines the credibility of the nursing profession. Upholding integrity ensures fair recognition of researchers, maintains institutional standards, and fosters a culture of truth in healthcare development.

headings.title: In-Text Citations Versus Reference Lists
headings.content:
Referencing requires two closely linked components working together: in-text citations and the reference list.

- **In-text citations**: Brief markers placed within the body of your text whenever you quote or paraphrase a source. They usually contain the author's last name and the year of publication.
- **Reference list**: A comprehensive list appearing at the very end of your paper, providing full publication details for every source cited in the text so readers can easily locate them.

headings.title: Major Referencing Styles in Healthcare
headings.content:
Different academic journals and nursing institutions use specific formatting styles to organize references. Choosing the correct style ensures consistency across professional literature.

| Style Name | Common Field | Typical In-Text Format |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **APA** | Nursing, Social Sciences | (Author, Year) |
| **Vancouver** | Medicine, Biomedical Sciences | Numeric superscript [1] |
| **Harvard** | General Sciences, Humanities | (Author, Year) |
| **MLA** | Humanities, Literature | (Author Page) |

Familiarity with APA (American Psychological Association) is most crucial for general nursing studies in Nigeria, while clinical medical journals frequently prefer Vancouver.

headings.title: Formatting Sources in APA Style
headings.content: APA style is widely used in nursing education. When citing a journal article with a single author in text, you write the author's surname followed by the publication year, such as (Okafor, 2022). For a book reference in your bibliography, the format follows the author's surname, initials, year, book title in italics, and publisher location. Pay close attention to punctuation, capital letters, and italics, as minor errors can affect the readability and formal presentation of your nursing project.

headings.title: Avoiding Plagiarism and Managing Citations
headings.content: Managing a large collection of references for a long research essay can become overwhelming. Reference management software such as Zotero, Mendeley, or EndNote helps students collect, organize, and automatically format citations in APA or Vancouver styles. However, software can sometimes generate errors if the original database entry contains mistakes. Always review your generated reference list manually before final submission. To avoid plagiarism, practice proper paraphrasing—expressing another author's ideas in your own unique sentence structure while retaining the original meaning and adding an accurate citation.
